title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
State Farm's lawyers submitted legal filings containing fabricated case citations, invented quotes, and false legal holdings generated by an AI tool called Irys. The lawyers discovered the false information only after opposing counsel flagged it. This is a model hallucination problem compounded by deployment without human verification, where an AI system asserted nonexistent legal authority as fact.

The failure occurred at the point of filing with a court. A lawyer used Irys to draft motions without checking whether the cases and quotations actually existed, apparently believing the tool was connected to legitimate legal research resources. Catching this would have required reviewing each citation against actual case law databases before submission, a standard practice in legal work that appears not to have happened.

It is not established whether this reflects failures in how Irys was designed, how the lawyer was trained to use it, or both.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
State Farm's defense lawyers apologized for submitting legal filings containing artificial intelligence-generated false information in a lawsuit brought by Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, a Los Angeles homeowner. The plaintiff's attorneys discovered that State Farm's motions included nonexistent cases, fabricated quotes, and invented legal holdings. Meni-Siliga sued State Farm and others in July 2024 after a 2020 fire made her Carson home uninhabitable, followed by water damage during repairs. She claims delays in getting State Farm's approval prevented completion of reconstruction work, leaving her family bankrupt and homeless after years of saving to purchase the property.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson acknowledged using an AI tool called Irys to prepare the filings and confirmed seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and misquoted material. She mistakenly believed Irys was connected to her firm's legal research subscription. Lead counsel Kenneth Katel apologized to the court and plaintiff, accepting responsibility despite not initially knowing AI was used. The case is scheduled for trial in October. This incident reflects broader concerns about AI hallucinations in legal work, as approximately 41 percent of law firms now use generative AI tools.
